extracted.intended_audience: journalism students (high-school and college) learning news lead and follow-up writing
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and principles for composing effective news leads and follow-up stories: how to summarize the gist, prioritize facts, answer the basic questions, and structure subsequent coverage so both prior readers and newcomers are served.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening sentence gives news briefly and concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Note how the opening sentence gives the news briefly and concretely with a few broad strokes, and how skillfully the questions who, what, where, when, why, how are answered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise, concrete opening that states the news in a few broad strokes and answers the basic journalistic questions (who, what, where, when, why, how). Example: front-page leads of the New York Times. Avoid long-winded, vague openings that bury the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer the questions who/what/where/when/why/how in the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: How skillfully the questions who, what, where, when, why, how are answered (in the opening sentence/lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the lead supplies the salient facts necessary for reader comprehension. If not all six can fit, prioritize the most newsworthy of them but aim to cover the core elements early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put what the reader is most interested in first
rubrics_metrics.description: NorE.—Remember that what we are most interested in goes first. Are you primarily interested in the librarian or in the Shakespeare collection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the primary focus of the story and lead with that element. This sets the angle and determines which facts are foregrounded. Test by asking: who/what is the story really about?

rubrics_metrics.name: Put the latest development first in follow-up stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The follow-up article must appeal to those who saw the first account and to those who did not. The lead, therefore, must include the latest development in the news with a summary of what preceded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the new information (latest development), then briefly summarize prior key facts so newcomers can understand context. Explicit rule: 'Put the Latest Development First.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Three valid ways to structure a follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Here are three ways to follow up the news: 1. Report the latest development. 2. Play up (that is, introduce and emphasize) a new phase of the event. 3. Play up an element that has been buried in previous follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning follow-ups, choose one of these approaches to give the story a clear purpose and avoid repetition. Each follow-up should add a distinct informational or interpretive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize concretely; put the news into the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: NorE.—Put the news into the lead. Summarize concretely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abstract or decorative openings. Compress the essential news into concrete language in the lead so readers immediately grasp the story's significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make general terms specific — avoid vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: The following is worthless as it stands because it is vague. Make the general terms specific or concrete so that the lead will give news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace generic phrases (e.g., 'this school', 'a number of years') with precise facts (names, dates, numbers, places) so the lead conveys real information rather than impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit unnecessary details from the lead; include only salient facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the elements given below into a lead. Omit any detail not necessary to the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing a lead, select and compress the elements that carry the news; background or minor details belong later in the story. Exercise: behead an article and write a lead — does it capture the salient facts?

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice concision: one-sentence summaries (≤30 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a sentence of not more than thirty words write a summary of each editorial in an afternoon paper that the class agrees to buy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, single-sentence summaries during drills to train economy and focus. Compare summaries to determine which best conveys the gist; this builds skill for tight leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up stories must serve both prior readers and newcomers
rubrics_metrics.description: The follow-up article must appeal to those who saw the first account and to those who did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the new development up front and a concise recap of prior key facts so returning readers learn what's new and new readers can follow the narrative without reading earlier pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt headline writing before studying headline principles; headline after story
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines are shown with some articles partly to preserve the spirit of the newspaper ... The head is prepared after the story is written. Headline writing should not be attempted by the student until he has made a study of the principles in Chapter XXIV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach headline composition only after students master lead and story principles. Prepare the headline after the story to ensure it reflects the finished copy and angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use drills (beheading, peer-lead writing, revision) to test lead effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring to class a short news story... Cut off the first paragraph. Give the 'beheaded' article to your neighbor who will write a lead for it. Compare the lead you hold with the lead he wrote. Did he put the salient facts into his lead? Did he accomplish what the original reporter did? Reread the stories you wrote after the lesson on the news story. In the light of your close-up study of the lead criticize and revise to your own satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular practice exercises and peer comparison are essential. Use beheading, lead-composition from supplied elements, and subsequent revision to internalize priorities (salience, concreteness, concision).
